sources.title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator — researchImpacts
sources.text: BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety. Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires. The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

sources.title: ACME BRE — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator — insight:bre-elevated-o2-no-flow
sources.text: Stopping ventilation may not be enough in oxygen-enriched cabins. In quiescent microgravity, BRE flames emulating condensed materials (e.g. PMMA, nylon) kept burning quasi-steadily in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas comparable flames at 21 % O2 self-extinguished in a short time. PSI describes these results as preliminary. Is ventilation shutdown — an established step in fighting spacecraft fires — still a sufficient first response at 26.5–34 % O2, or must agent discharge come sooner?

sources.title: SAFFIRE-I — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I — researchImpacts
sources.text: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions.

sources.title: SAFFIRE-II — Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II — insight:saffire2-ug-vs-1g
sources.text: Microgravity and 1-g rankings of materials can disagree. In SAFFIRE-II, 4 of 4 silicone samples (0.27–1.03 mm) had a burn length of about 0 in microgravity at 20 cm/s, while 2 of the 4 matching 1-g reference burns were complete. Flames did spread in microgravity over: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric). A 1-g screening result can be optimistic for some materials (BASS hypothesis) and pessimistic for others — which materials of a given vehicle need microgravity testing?

top_passage.text: To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.
